events.title: Roboflow
events.description:
Roboflow: Building a Real-Time Computer Vision Checkout with Python

Computer vision has become more accessible than ever, but what does it take to build a complete, real-time application from camera to customer?

Join Pyowa on Tuesday, August 25th, as Zac Crane presents "Roboflow." In this session, Zac will demonstrate a computer vision project that uses Python to recognize concession stand items and calculate an order total in real time.

You'll get a behind-the-scenes look at how Python and Roboflow work together to connect a camera feed, edge computing, an object detection model, pricing logic, and WebSocket communication that instantly sends the running total to a phone display. Along the way, Zac will share lessons learned while building an end-to-end computer vision application that bridges machine learning and real-world software engineering.

As always, we'll wrap up with time for questions, discussion, and networking with fellow members of the Pyowa community.
Join us from 5:30-7pm hosted at Source Allies. Food, drinks, and great conversation are included.

events.title: Pybites Coding Exercises
events.description:
Pyowa returns on Tuesday, September 22nd from 5:30-7pm for a hands-on evening of Python coding with “Pybites Coding Exercises.”

Instead of a traditional presentation, this meetup will give attendees time to work through coding exercises using Pybites, experiment with different approaches, and learn alongside other members of the local Python community.

Bring your laptop and work through challenges independently or pair with others! The evening is an opportunity to sharpen your skills, practice problem-solving, and learn from fellow developers.

Hosted in person at Source Allies. Food and drinks provided.

events.title: Fraud Detection on the Elliptic Bitcoin Dataset: Graphs, Leakage, and Topology
events.description:
Pyowa returns to Source Allies on Tuesday, October 27th from 5:30–7pm with Dave Keller presenting a hands-on look at fraud detection, machine learning, and the importance of questioning results that seem a little too good.

In this session, Dave will explore his work using the Elliptic Bitcoin transaction dataset to investigate fraud detection. When his initial models produced near-perfect performance, it raised an important question: was the model actually learning meaningful patterns, or was data leakage influencing the results?

Dave will walk through rebuilding the experiment with a temporal train/validation/test split and establishing logistic regression and Random Forest baselines. He’ll also cover how statistical techniques including Spearman correlation, mutual information, and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests helped investigate relationships between features and time.

Rather than chasing the highest possible model score, this talk is about questioning results, testing alternative explanations, and understanding what the evidence does and does not support.

Hosted at Source Allies. Food and drinks will be provided.

Speaker Bio: Dave is a court researcher and aspiring data scientist with a background in mathematics. He is currently pursuing the MITx MicroMasters in Statistics and Data Science and develops projects focused on machine learning, fraud detection, graph analytics, and Python.
